analysis.one_liner: Raises the child tax credit to $5,000 per child and makes it fully refundable with no income limit.
analysis.headline: A bill to raise the child tax credit to $5,000 per child and make it fully refundable has sat untouched in committee since February 2025, with no cosponsors and no action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the child tax credit from its current amount to $5,000 per child, make it fully refundable so that families who owe little or no income tax get the full amount as cash back, and remove all income limits so high earners qualify too. It was introduced by Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in February 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children, especially low- and middle-income ones. The bill would raise the child tax credit to $5,000 per child [S2] and make it fully refundable, meaning families who owe little or no income tax would receive the full amount as a refund — today many poor families get only a partial credit or none at all [S2]. Removing the income limitations means no family is phased out of the credit [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with children, especially low-income ones

how_it_helps.text: Raises the child tax credit to $5,000 per child, a large increase over the credit's statutory base amount [S2].
Makes the credit fully refundable, so families with little or no income tax liability receive the full amount rather than a reduced portion [S2].
Removes the income phase-out limitations entirely, so no family loses the credit because its income rises [S2].
Applies to tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury — meaning current and future taxpayers — since the bill contains no revenue offsets and expands the credit to every family with children regardless of income, which would substantially increase federal deficits unless paired with spending cuts or tax increases elsewhere.

drawbacks.text: The bill removes all income limitations, meaning the wealthiest families would also collect the full $5,000 per child, which greatly increases the cost of the credit and directs part of the benefit to households that need it least [S2].
The bill includes no offsetting revenue — no spending cuts or tax increases — so the entire expansion would be deficit-financed, adding substantially to federal debt [S2].
The bill has no cosponsors, suggesting little appetite even among the sponsor's colleagues for its specific design [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — a larger, fully refundable child credit — would deliver real money to families with children, and refundability is what makes the credit reach the poorest families at all. But this version is designed without discipline: no income limits and no funding source mean an enormous, open-ended cost, much of it flowing to high-income households who would get the full credit regardless. A narrower, paid-for version would help far more per dollar. As written, it is a statement bill rather than a workable one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a vote, or even a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie introduced the bill on February 18, 2025, proposing a $5,000 fully refundable child tax credit with no income limits [S1] [S2].
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the same day, which is the standard first stop for tax legislation [S4].
No other member of the House has cosponsored the bill [S3].
The committee has held no hearing, markup, or vote, and the bill has not reached the House floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained yet. Families with children would benefit if the bill moved, but for now the only thing that has happened is referral to a committee that has not acted on it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill has not advanced

for.name: Rep. Ryan Mackenzie
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which was then referred to committee

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith)
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no other member has signed on, so the partisan shape of support is unknown; the single sponsor is a Republican.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors and no committee action months after introduction, this bill is almost certain to die quietly in the Ways and Means Committee, as most single-sponsor tax bills do. It could advance only if folded into a larger tax package or if its sponsor builds broader support, neither of which is in evidence.
